item.title: 5-Year-Old Dies After Digital Whiteboard Falls in School Classroom
item.description:
A 5-year-old student at a Florida elementary school died on Wednesday after a 120-pound video display board fell on him in his classroom, the school district said.

Bellamy Dawkins-Morris was seriously injured when a digital board fell on him just after 11:30 a.m. at Riviera Elementary School in Palm Bay, about 70 miles southeast of Orlando, the Palm Bay Police Department said. School staff members called 911 and administered first aid until emergency responders arrived, law enforcement officials said, but Bellamy died after being transported to a hospital.

Brevard Public Schools, the school district, said in a statement on Thursday that the large video display had been mounted on a wall by a licensed third-party vendor in accordance with manufacturer guidelines. The board was made by Promethean, an education technology company, and the district said all of its boards made by the company were being inspected.

“The safety and well-being of our students and staff remain our highest priority,” Dr. Mark Rendell, the superintendent for Brevard Public Schools, said in the statement. “We will continue to work closely with law enforcement, take appropriate precautions to ensure the safety of our school communities, and provide additional information when it becomes available and appropriate to share.”

Promethean said in a statement that it was also investigating the incident.

Family members told the local TV news station WESH 2, an NBC affiliate, that Bellamy had been moving the display board back and forth while other students were lining up when it tipped over and fell on him. The family told the local news network that Bellamy was autistic.

“When he sees things in motion, he’s going to keep pushing it to keep it in motion; that’s just something that children on the spectrum do,” Miriam Rodriguez, Bellamy’s great-aunt, told WESH 2. “Obviously, the monitor was not secure, and that’s a huge issue. That could have been anybody’s child.”

The Palm Bay Police Department said its special victims unit was investigating the incident.

Dr. Rendell, the superintendent, said at a news conference on Wednesday that he had met with Bellamy’s family shortly after the child’s death.

“We lost a life today, a precious young life. There are no words to describe that loss,” Dr. Rendell said. “I’ve been doing this for over 30 years, and I really couldn’t find the words to share with them my grief and the grief that all of us have.”

Promethean displays are used in classrooms around the world, sometimes in lieu of traditional blackboards. The interactive panels display lesson plans and have touch-screen features.

“All of us at Promethean are heartbroken by the death of a child in the tragic accident at Riviera Elementary School,” a spokesman for Promethean said in a statement. “Nothing matters more to us than the safety of the students and teachers who use our products every day.”

item.title: Pentagon Draws Up New Iran Strike Plans as Trump Hesitates
item.description:
The U.S. military is preparing options to restart major combat operations against Iran, even as President Trump continues to show ambivalence about restarting the war, according to American officials.

Three aircraft carriers will soon be in the Middle East, a massive assembly of force, and the Pentagon, on Mr. Trump’s orders, has developed plans to strike Iran’s drone and missile arsenal, energy facilities and other military sites.

But Mr. Trump has repeatedly decided not to relaunch heavy combat operations against Iran. And the U.S. military response to Iran has been more muted in recent weeks, despite Iran’s escalating attacks on oil tankers.

In a social media post on Thursday, Mr. Trump said that he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, and that the two countries were “having productive discussions.”

In recent months, officials said, Mr. Trump’s national security team and the Pentagon have made five proposals to him for major operations against either Iran or the Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia based in Yemen. Each time, Mr. Trump vetoed the plans.

But Mr. Trump has once more ordered up strike options. Senior national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed plans at a meeting last Friday at Camp David. The plans center on a short, intense campaign lasting about three days, according to people briefed on the proposal.

The strikes would focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has rebuilt since the early phase of the war. Other targets could include Iranian energy facilities and Revolutionary Guard command posts and headquarters.

The latest plans were earlier reported by Axios.

Officials have backed Mr. Trump’s assessment that some progress is being made in diplomatic talks, which have continued through mediators. The talks have continued to get hung up on the issue of Iran’s nuclear program. American officials want to reach a deal on Iran’s nuclear ambitions first, while Iranian negotiators insist that those discussions must come last.

Over the months, Iran has become a tougher opponent as its military tactics improved. Taking down Iranian missiles has required more interceptors than earlier in the war, posing challenges to America’s already taxed arsenal of munitions. Armed with satellite imagery from Chinese companies, Iran has also been able to more effectively target U.S. bases, according to people briefed on the intelligence.

Since September, the time of the last significant exchange of retaliatory attacks, Iran has struck at least 13 ships, according to a monitoring group run by the British Navy. Intelligence reports have put the number higher, at nearly 20, according to people briefed on the information. None of those attacks generated a major U.S. response.

While oil exports from the Middle East are up, Iran’s increased attacks have spooked shippers and raised questions about future energy shipments.

Throughout the summer, the U.S. military regularly retaliated after Iranian attacks on international shipping. But the far less robust response since then reflects Mr. Trump’s hesitancy to restart the war in full, officials say.

U.S. commanders are also concerned about the increasing difficulty of stopping Iranian attacks against bases where American troops are stationed, and energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in the region.

On Thursday, in his social media post, Mr. Trump insisted that none of the oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz was coming from Iran. That is debatable, according to people briefed on intelligence reports. Iran allows some vessels to pass that have paid fees or that potentially carry some of its oil. Iran also has its own dark fleet of tankers, according to current and former officials.

Chinese companies have paid fees to Iran to transit the strait, and Iran has long secretly blended its oil with Iraqi oil to avoid sanctions. The Treasury Department on Thursday sanctioned 17 vessels that it said were part of Iran’s shadow fleet smuggling oil.

Even members of Mr. Trump’s inner circle are increasingly skeptical that military action will change Tehran’s calculus or plans. Some of these officials believe that the Trump administration’s campaign of economic pressure is working and just needs more time to force Iran to make meaningful concessions.

Even before Mr. Trump said there would be no strike before the November vote, officials had predicted that he would wait until after the Israeli elections, on Oct. 27, and the U.S. midterms the following week to decide whether to attack.

But U.S. military commanders are ready to begin larger operations in the coming days, in case the president shifts again.

The Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left San Diego last week and will join the George H.W. Bush and the George Washington carriers as early as the end of October. Each strike group includes other warships carrying attack helicopters and Marines. It will be the first time since 2003 that three aircraft carriers will be in the Middle East.

At the end of the month, there will be more than 20,000 sailors and Marines afloat, along with hundreds of aircraft. But the high troop level will be only temporary. The George Washington is expected to return to its base in Japan soon after the Roosevelt arrives next month to replace it.

Despite the force buildup, it is hardly certain that Mr. Trump will give a green light to any new attacks even after the election. Senior U.S. officials are worried about further depleting the global arsenal of defensive weapons to defend bases in the Middle East, as well as the U.S. ability to intercept Iranian attacks.

Still other officials in favor of resumed operations note that Iran’s economy continues to weaken, and a short, intense barrage could intensify Tehran’s problems, especially if it hurts Iran’s ability to control the strait, according to current and former officials.

The United States has continued to take out Iranian drones and cruise missiles. But it has not attacked Iran’s dark tanker fleet or conducted retaliatory strikes inside Iran.

At the beginning of the war, the U.S. military in most cases fired two interceptors at incoming Iranian missiles, focusing on the most dangerous volleys.

But American officials now say Iran’s improved tactics and targeting have forced the United States and its regional partners to fire more missiles to thwart salvos aimed at American bases in the region.

American commanders say they still have reserves of interceptors as the war has drained stockpiles, and U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has pulled in weaponry from Europe and Asia.

Reporting was contributed by Jonathan Swan and Alan Rappeport in Washington; David E. Sanger in Cambridge, Mass.; and Farnaz Fassihi in New York.

item.title: 21 Birds Are Found at Miami Airport Stuffed in Underwear and Hidden in a Belt
item.description:
Twice this week, men arrived at Miami International Airport from Havana and aroused the suspicions of customs officers for the same reason.

Something seemed to be concealed beneath their clothing.

The something, they found, turned out to be clutches of live birds hidden on their persons. In one of the arrests, 10 birds were stuffed in the man’s underpants, according to charging documents. The other man was smuggling 11 birds.

That man, Alberto Hernandez Castillo, disembarked from his flight on Sunday in a pair of gold-sheened sneakers, according to a criminal complaint. He appeared nervous and authorities observed an “unexplained bulge” around his pelvis.

The second man, Roberto Perez Quincosa, 41, who arrived on Tuesday, was also arrested after officials made similar observations about him.

Each man was charged with smuggling.

Authorities have not said if the cases were related. A lawyer for Mr. Hernandez Castillo did not respond to a request for comment. It was unknown if Mr. Perez Quincosa had a lawyer.

A pat-down found that Mr. Hernandez Castillo had black pouches sewn into his underpants, according to an account in the complaint from a special agent with Homeland Security Investigations. Nestled inside were six slim tubes, bound in beige tape and affixed with black mesh at the opening. Each contained one or two breathing birds, the complaint said.

Mr. Perez Quincosa had devised a belt-like garment to hold the 11 birds he carried, according to an account from a special agent with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that was included in a criminal complaint. He had used hair roller tubes “with holes along their length and capped with netting material,” wrapped in electrical tape, the complaint said.

Some of the birds that were recovered, such as the two blue grosbeaks that the authorities said Mr. Castillo had on him, are protected species. Eight yellow-faced grassquits were also found on him. Mr. Perez Quincosa had transported six Cuban melodious finches and five Cuban bullfinches, according to the complaint.

Yellow-faced grassquits are native to South and Central America and are named for the bands of yellow above the eyes and across the throats of males. Blue grosbeaks are North American songbirds.

Mr. Hernandez Castillo and Mr. Perez Quincosa were both born in Cuba and are now permanent U.S. residents, according to the complaints. Neither had filed the appropriate paperwork to legally import wildlife into the United States, and they had also checked “no” on customs declarations forms when asked if they were bringing animals or wildlife into the country.

Mr. Hernandez Castillo was released on Monday after posting a $25,000 bond, according to court records. The authorities did not say on Thursday if Mr. Perez Quincosa was still in custody.

Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Customs and Border Protection referred inquiries to the Fish and Wildlife Service, which said in an email that it could not comment because it was still investigating.

The authorities did not say what happened to the birds, although trafficked animals sometimes are handed over to a zoo or shelter.

Miami is a gateway for smugglers seeking to bring wildlife into the United States from Latin America and the Caribbean, many of them to be offered for sale. The World Wildlife Fund estimates that, globally, as many as 1.5 million birds have been trafficked in a single year. Exotic birds with colorful plumage can sell for a thousand dollars or more. Global profits can reach the tens of billions of dollars, according to Bird Life International, a conservation group.

Last year, a man crossed from Mexico into California with two sedated parrots hidden in his trousers. In 2018, at least 200 finches made their way from South to North America stuffed in plastic hair rollers or in luggage. And six years before that, Interpol raids on airports, post offices pet stores and other settings in 32 countries uncovered more than 8,000 wild animals, most of them birds.

According to the complaints, Mr. Perez Quincosa told law enforcement that he knew bringing in the birds was unlawful and that he intended to breed and sell them for $100 to $120 each. Mr. Hernandez Castillo said that the birds he was carrying were intended for his “personal use,” according to the complaint. He then invoked his right to remain silent.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Army Actions Contributed to Reagan Airport Collision, Internal Report Says
item.description:
Army investigators have concluded that problems with military training and helicopter technology contributed to a midair collision between an Army Black Hawk helicopter and a passenger jet that killed 67 people last year.

The internal report, copies of which were provided to reporters by relatives of crash victims Thursday, included recommendations to improve deficiencies that investigators said played a role in the January 2025 incident near Ronald Reagan National Airport, which is just outside of Washington. The episode prompted federal investigations and a national debate about aviation safety.

Like the National Transportation Safety Board, the independent federal agency that investigates aviation accidents, Army investigators found that the helicopter’s location-broadcasting technology had not been functioning properly on the night of the incident. They also concluded that officials had known that the helicopter’s altitude gauges could give faulty readings.

They recommended technology upgrades and urged that certain military aircraft be required to turn on location-broadcasting software while operating flights through the Washington area, “except when supporting an actual national security contingency.” They did not specify what constituted such an occurrence.

Safety advocates, lawmakers and the families of victims have been calling for stricter laws to prevent collisions between military aircraft and commercial flights around the busiest U.S. airports. Army investigators suggested in their report that the military was capable of self-regulating, and did not need new laws.

“Aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky,” Families of Flight 5342, a group formed among the relatives of those who died in the crash, said in a statement. “The technology is proven. All that’s required is the political will to do the right thing.”

The group added: “There is nothing left for Congress to wait for.”

The Army did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The pilots operating the Army Black Hawk involved in the collision were flying a national security training mission the night of the accident. Since then, the Federal Aviation Administration has changed the route the Army helicopter had been flying along near Reagan National and limited helicopter activity in the area to only critical emergency or military missions, such as transporting the president.

Lawmakers are currently debating whether such restrictions should be codified, as part of legislation to mandate the use of advanced technology.

The Army’s report agreed with N.T.S.B. recommendations urging leaders to create a database for reporting and analyzing incidents, to better understand the risks of flying through dense, complex airspace, and to offer more training to pilots operating flights in those areas.

But it differs from the N.T.S.B. on whether its own pilots might have erred on the night of the accident.

The N.T.S.B. determined that the helicopter pilots likely made a mistake when asking air traffic controllers at Reagan National for permission to fly through the area relying on their own ability to see and avoid obstacles. Army investigators, however, did not find evidence that the helicopter crew ignored any information.

Rather, they blamed the air traffic controller for insufficiently warning the pilots that they were on a collision course.

item.title: Fort Hood Shooter’s Execution Will be Public and Streamed Live, Pentagon Says
item.description:
Pentagon officials said on Thursday that the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting would be executed in public, a practice that ended in the United States nearly a century ago and is most commonly carried out in a handful of countries including Iran, North Korea and the Taliban-led government in Afghanistan.

The Pentagon said in a statement that the military execution, scheduled for Dec. 3, would also be broadcast via livestream. Such a broadcast has little precedent, and releasing video of executions is most often associated with extremist militant groups like the Islamic State.

The announcement adds to the growing spectacle around the planned execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others when he brought a personal handgun onto the grounds of Fort Hood, Texas. The rampage was the deadliest shooting at an American military base and sent shock waves through the U.S. military.

There are few countries that hold public executions. The human rights group Amnesty International has highlighted some cases in which public executions in Iran and Saudi Arabia have been filmed by bystanders.

The practice of filming and releasing video of an execution is more common with terror groups like the Islamic State, which became infamous for videos of gruesome executions of prisoners who were not given due process or convicted of crimes. Mass shooters have in some cases broadcast their killing sprees on livestream sites.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet, aboard the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the execution would be public and available to watch “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” The Pentagon later confirmed in a statement that the execution would be livestreamed.

The Army has said the public execution of Major Hasan will be conducted by firing squad at Fort Hood, the site of the shooting. If carried out, it would be a first in modern American history.

The last state-sanctioned public execution in the United States occurred more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky. Some 20,000 people gathered to witness the August 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea, a young Black man who had been convicted of raping an elderly white woman.

Major Hasan’s execution would be the first by the military justice system since 1961, and he would be the first soldier put to death by firing squad since World War II. The firing squad is a rare method of execution, but one that has been used by the military, particularly during wartime. The Trump administration has proposed expanding its use as a method of execution.

Mr. Hegseth said that the decision to shoot Major Hasan by a firing squad, as well as other details of the execution, were chosen for their symbolism.

“Of course we’re going to do it at Fort Hood,” Mr. Hegseth said. “And do it on a Thursday and we’re going to do it at 1 o’clock — which is when he did it — and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad. It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that.”

He continued, “Well I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II.”

On Nov. 5, 2009, Major Hasan, an Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood, brought a personal handgun onto the base grounds and opened fire. Major Hasan said that he carried out the attack, which occurred at the height of the post-9/11 fight against terrorism, to wage jihad for what he called the illegal and immoral wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. He admitted to the killings during his court-martial and was convicted in 2013 of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

Major Hasan, who was wounded in the shooting, is being held at the military death row prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kan. He expressed no remorse for his actions, and told a military mental health panel that he wished he had died in the attack so that he could have become a martyr.

Mr. Hegseth and other Pentagon officials emphasized Major Hasan’s motivations for the shooting in their public statements about the execution. Mr. Hegseth also criticized President Barack Obama for not describing the attack at the time as an act of terror.

Speaking at a rally in Texas on Wednesday, Mr. Trump, a vocal advocate of the death penalty, trumpeted his order to execute Major Hasan, telling the crowd in San Antonio that “we are going to deliver final justice to an evil killer.”

item.title: How Trump Has Alienated G.O.P. Voters
item.description:
I have been talking to working-class Americans about their political preferences since 2016, and have written many stories about how Donald Trump inspired them. Now, after 10 years, a war and sky-high fuel prices, more and more working-class Americans I am talking to are saying they’ve had enough.

Like Jim Pasek, 80, a retired pharma plant custodian, who loved Trump in the early years but now says, “He’s not making sense.” Or Sebastian Covey, 24, a landscaper, who cast a ballot for Trump in the first vote of his life and now is scrambling to find a carpool partner after swapping his truck for a car to cope with the rising cost of gas.

Many Americans still support Trump. But something is happening to his support that I have not seen since he took the political establishment by storm a decade ago.

One statistic from our public opinion poll last month that I find particularly relevant: Just 29 percent of likely Republican voters said the economy was better than it had been a year ago, down from 72 percent in January.

That sentiment is settling into this midterm election, dragging down Republican enthusiasm in a pattern that the independent political analyst Charlie Cook has termed the “red undertow.” Cook points out that it does not mean these disenchanted Republicans will vote for Democrats. Most will not. As Lindsay Kronemeyer, a 35-year-old Christian conservative, told me, “My belief system is still the same.” Instead, Cook argues, the dynamic will be a hindrance for Republican candidates, particularly in close races.

But Kronemeyer, an up-and-coming member of the Republican Party in Michigan who canvassed for Trump in 2016 and in 2020, wants to think about the party’s future. And Trump, she says, is not part of it. “He’s just not there in my head anymore,” she told me.

Debate Week

The main event last night was in Iowa, where Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican candidate for Senate, and State Representative Josh Turek, her Democratic opponent, sparred “politely but sharply,” as Bayliss Wagner wrote.

A couple of Bayliss’s takeaways from the debate:

The Iran war, and its fallout, was a major issue. Hinson has voted against resolutions to rein in Trump’s war powers, and Turek sought to capitalize on it, telling voters, “When you’re struggling at the pump, that is because of Ashley Hinson.” Hinson tried to thread the needle between support for Trump and concern over the war, saying the conflict needed to come to “an immediate and successful end.”

Both candidates highlighted their bipartisanship. Turek, who was once a registered Republican, emphasized that he had voted hundreds of times with Republicans in the State House, while Hinson promoted her work with the Democratic former House speaker Nancy Pelosi.

The schedule picks up, with debates in Michigan, Maine and Georgia. They’ll offer a glimpse of three very different election landscapes: In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, looks so solid that Republicans have pulled back on TV ads, while in Maine, the incumbent Republican, Senator Susan Collins, has been looking stronger in polls.

And in Michigan, the race between Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers appears to be neck and neck. We’ll be covering that one live. Follow along here.

Get Caught Up

Trump was in San Antonio last night to pump up Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. But his speech seemed more focused on getting voters excited about Trump himself, writes Shawn McCreesh. (And, as usual, Trump insulted Paxton’s appearance.)

In the hours before the Michigan debate, Trump referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” in a Truth Social post. El-Sayed responded, “He knows my name is Abdul,” and said the president was trying to distract voters from his unpopular policies.

Trump will hold a rally in Alaska next week to boost the re-election campaigns of Senator Dan Sullivan and Representative Nick Begich, who are locked in competitive races.

As the temperature drops, Mainers are stressing. That’s because half the homes in Maine rely on oil for heat, and the war in Iran has caused prices to surge.

The issue is moving to the center of the Senate race. Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate, brought it up at a town hall event this week, joking that people might have to get creative in heating their homes if they can’t shell out money for oil.
